title: Billy McBride and Mary McBride ("Mack and Mack") Interview, 1959-07-01
interviewee: Billy McBride and Mary McBride ("Mack and Mack")

blocks.x: 된
된 된 된
된
된
된 smack and mac. Yes. And where were you born? Can you tell? Oh, I was born in Mobile, Alabama in the year of 1884. You have the exact date, if you don't mind. February the 26th. Nice to have

that, too. It happened to be on a Mardi Gras day. Oh, Mardi Gras day. They have quite a Mardi Gras in Mobile, too. In Mobile, yes. Pensacola also. And this is McBride. Where were you born? In Algiers,
Louisiana. That's West New Orleans. On July the 28th, 1891. That makes me 68 this birthday.

Yes. 28th of July. Before I forget it, I don't think I'll forget it, but Professor Minetta has mentioned Mary Mack. I didn't know if you were known by that name. Mary Mack, yes. At that time. He mentioned that Mary Mack came from Algiers and was a wonderful singer and entertainer. I know he would send his regards. He didn't know I was going to see you. Well, I'd be glad. And I see him almost every Tuesday night. I go over to his studio where he teaches and I record a little interview with him. I see. And when he teaches some of his lessons, talking about music, too. Yes. He's still active. Oh, I'm so glad to hear that. So he'll be glad to hear your voice. If you don't mind, I'll play him this tape sometime. I think he would enjoy
hearing your voice again. Well, I would be glad for you to play, for him to hear. Me and Mac. Yes, and we had, we were known in show business as Mary Mack's Merry Makers. Oh, yes.

Uh-huh. That record that you made with Kid Punch is called that, I remember. The Merry Makers Twine? Well, oh, that, no, that was a Lovie Austin record, wasn't it? No, Lovie Austin played it, but that's our record. I know. I mean, she made a record of it once. Yes. Oh, yes, she did. That's

quite a while back. Now, what did that mean, that Merry Makers Twine? Well, you can see here, this is the name of the company. We call it at first, the Southern Comedy Company, but after we got a little better organized and more people added to the show, we named it after the wife, Mary. Oh, yes.

Mac's Merry Makers. Mary Mac's Merry Makers Company. Oh, yes. And Billy Mac presents that twirly-girly jazz comedy Jubilee. That's it? Yeah. This was the little program that... That we had, yes. You had. This was back in 19... No? 26. 1926. At that, yes. In November. Yes. Which city was this in? I think that was in Youngstown, Ohio.
Federal Street, yes. I don't recognize. Yeah, Federal Street. That's the Prince's Theatre. Oh, yes. Here it tells on the front.
Prince's Family Theatre, Youngstown, Ohio. Now, can you tell me when you first met your wife, Mr. Brian? Oh, yes. It was in

the year of... 19... 1908. 1909. Were you in the entertainment field? Oh, yes. I started out with this little company that she joined later in 1908, but I didn't actually meet her until 1909. And I took the company out with all men, all boys. Of course, I was not a boy myself. Yes, sir. But I somehow, I had a... No show people in my family, but I just had that inclination to be a showman. And I got together these boys and started out with a little menstrual style show, which later became a kind of a presentation show. Yes. And we didn't have any girls whatsoever until we met a man that was stranded down in a little town called Bay St. Louis, Mississippi. Oh, yes, I know that. You do. And there was a little theater there, and he had the theater in charge, but he couldn't carry on so very well. I mean, we joined up with the theater. And, uh, uh, coming around the town that we still wanted to make the show a little larger. In fact, we needed a girl that could talk. And so I went to New Orleans to see if we could get some girls, which was about 51 miles from Bay St. Louis. And that's where I met my wife. Somebody directed me to this girl. And I found her early one morning after she had come from a singing engagement out at the fairgrounds, was it?
Lincoln Park. Oh, yeah, Lincoln Park. Yeah. Yes.

Did you play or sing with Robichaux out there? Yes. I know he played there for many years. Buddy Bartley, he did the balloon ascension. Yes. Professor Minetta has told us all about those too. Yes. Yes. One time he went up too far and, uh, and he got lost. He went over in the lake. Yes, yes, yes, yes.

Well, then that's how we met. And then, uh, we went to Bay St. Louis. He taken me to Bay St. Louis. And, uh, then we went to Mobile and that's where we married. Mobile, Alabama. In 1909, about? In 1909. We've been together. The Haley's Comet was along that line there. I remember that. When I was a boy is one of the first things I can remember.
Yeah. And I was in my teens then, you know. Yeah. It was just, just, uh, 18th Wednesday had just passed

about then. Can you tell me more about your act? Just, I know you sang. All I know is the record that you made with Punch. And one other question I wanted to ask while I think of it. There was a record with Louis Armstrong. I tried to get every record that Armstrong ever made. And there was one with a Baby Mac singing. Now, was that you? That little Baby Mac. That wasn't me. No relation? No. No relation. No relation.
I wondered. Well, now, uh, uh, we, uh, uh, in 1914, that's the first time we supposed to come up north,

you know. We went to Memphis, Tennessee. Wasn't it, Matt? Yeah. No, we went to Memphis in 1911. 1911. But it was 1914 when we'd come back to New Orleans and organized this company. And then went to New York. Yes. And went everywhere along the lines, stopping in different towns. And at that time, we didn't have any booking agents. We'd just write to the theater managers that we could hear of. Book yourself directly. Just book direct all the way along from New Orleans to New York. Later, there was that T.O.B.A. were you ever on that? Oh, we stayed on that. We organized it, yeah. We really helped organize it. We knew, uh, Mr. Dudley, S.H. Dudley, and, uh, Mr. Sam Reaven of Chattanooga, Tennessee, and, uh, Mr. Klein, Martin Klein of Chicago. And Bailey. Yeah, Bailey in Atlanta. And Tim Osley of, uh, uh, Indianapolis, they got together to organize this and they first called it, uh, the, uh, uh, uh, Dudley-Dudley-Kline Circuit. But they later called it the Theater Owners Booking Association. Yes. And, uh, we were in there at all that. We did a vaudeville act for them around just a team, singing, dancing, and talking. Yeah. And, uh, we played all these towns, first from New, New Orleans into New York and back as a team. And we went back later and organized this company. That's when I got
Johnny Dodds and- Well, that's what I wanted to hear about. Mud Carey told me he came up to Chicago with you.
Yes, yes. And the drummer was Little Mac, Mud Carey on the trumpet. What was his last name? Do you remember? I think his last name was Robinson, but did we call him? Robinson. Yes. Little Mac

Robinson. There was once a Mac Murray there. Yeah. And then I've heard of a Mac Hill that Lee Collins has told me about. It wouldn't be Mac Hill. Oh, no, no, no, no. I didn't know any of those fellas myself, personally. Well, they all were kids. But Roberts. You think it was Mac Robertson? I think
it was Mac Robertson because- Or Robinson or Robertson? Robinson. Robinson.

Yeah, if I'm not sure. Because we'd call him Little Mac. Little Mac, yes. I've heard him call. Yeah. And then we had Steve Lewis. On piano. Yes. Steve Lewis was on piano. Johnny Dodds on clarinet, and Mud Carey on the cornet. Well, who was a trombone player? Well, at that time, he only brought four. That's what Mud told me. Only four pieces that you came up. And we were the first company that had the jazz band on the stage, isn't it? That's right, yes. On the stage. Not down in the pit, we put them on the stage. Oh, you did? I didn't know. That's where it was. Right here at the Monogram Theater. About what year?
Do you remember? 1918. 1918. That's when the flu was. Oh, yes. I remember. I had the... Yes. Do you remember?

Oh, that's when almost the stage was signed, we were here. Yeah, we were here all through that time, but we stayed there quite a while. Yes. And we used to stay as long as two years, you know, at this one theater. That was on 31st Street? Yes, 35th. 35th. Monogram is 35th. The monogram?
The new monogram. Uh-huh. The old monogram was up to 35th, but they didn't have any
border to that. I never got to see that. I knew some of the theaters, like the Grand,

and they tore that down just a few weeks ago, I hear. And we had the style of presenting the show, was what they later called a presentation, but at the time, I didn't name it that, but there was a man downtown at the Oriental Theater called Paul Ash. Oh, yes. And he come out to the monogram and saw the style of show I was doing, and he took it downtown, and he got credit for
this presentation show. I remember I was here in 1924 studying music, and he had a show at the McVickers then. Yes, yes. And you originated that style of presentation. I really did. And the Royal
Garden Blues, now uh. Clarence Williams wrote that. Yes, Clarence Williams, he wrote that. And I, uh, they,

I featured it before it was published. You know, when I first met Jimmy Noon, or one of the first times I saw him back about 1937 or 38, I'm quite sure Jimmy told me that he helped write that, that they, he and Joe Oliver and some members of the band worked that out. Yes, yes. Over at Royal Garden. At the Royal Garden. But Clarence Williams, I guess, bought it and published it. Did you know anything about it? No, no, no, no.
He didn't buy it. He wrote that, and she sung it at Pete Lalla's Cabaret. Clarence Williams really worked on the number of that.
stuff Then I featured it here on the stage at the Money Graham and Joe Oliver and then there's St. Louis Armstrong and Lil and all of those people at the Royal Garden and that's where we featured it.
You appeared at the Royal Garden too?

Yes, over on Carys Grove. She did. See, I at that time, this was a little later, say a couple of years, we went back down south and come back to Chicago, worked our way down and back again. We played the Grand Theater which was owned by Mr. Miller, the man that owned these monograms. He sent her to the Royal Garden.

Well, I was here for my little girl to be born, you know. She was four weeks old, that's when I went. Before I went back, I went down in Texas to take her down there for Mac to see her. But that's when I worked at the Lincoln, at the Royal Garden.
Were you sort of like the band vocalist that they have now or was it a special act? I never did know much about the Royal Garden. I never got to go there when it was open.

No, you didn't have a vocal like that. The performers would entertain in the center of the floor. And Joe Oliver and them would play. Was that more like a nightclub or a dance hall? Yes, like a nightclub. I didn't know if it was a dance. And dance hall. People did dance too. Yes, yes. You entertained on the floor. I see.
The band was elevated.

Yes, you entertained on the floor instead of going up there to sing through the mic like the entertainers do now. You'd go around to the tables and then your dancer, the chorus would come out in the center of the floor and dance. And it was our chorus from the show.
I see. I always wondered about the Royal Garden if it was just a dance hall where you pay admission or go in and buy drinks or what it was like. No, no.
It was that entertainment. But a flow show and dancing.

I did once go to the Dreamland. Richard M. Jones took me over to the Dreamland. I remember they had a big glass or mirror or something in the floor there too. She worked there. Did you work there too?
Yes, I worked there too. Well, and Willie Umfrey. Do you know him?
Is that the young Willie Umfrey? His father was named Willie too.
Yes, but the father was a father. We used to call him Little Belly. He was so fat, you know. They both play clarinet. Yes.
They're both living too. Uh-huh.
Well, they had one son that played trombone.
Yes, Earl. Earl Umfrey. We brought him here too.
We brought him, yeah.

And Percy, the drummer, now plays the trumpet. He's the leader of the Eureka Brass Band in New Orleans. He's still active. Both of them are active. Earl plays bass. He's over in Virginia. I've never met him.
We brought Umfrey here too. The old man.
The old man.
The old man. We brought him here too.
Oh, by the way, Talk On, I just want to, I made a list of some of the people. You maybe even think of more.
Oh, yeah.
Now the different piano players that we had from time to time from now. About stuff
The first was Johnny King, he was of Mobile of course, then Clarence Williams, George Thomas, Maroney Jones, which is Richard Jones of course, Buddy Christian.
Yes, he's in New York, I think he may be dead now I believe.
Yeah, and Bud Scott used to be our, with us.

Well I got him down here too. L.C. Tolan, now that's a piano player, oh yes, and Jimmy Clark, of course he wasn't of New Orleans, neither was James Alston, Gus Ivory, was from Birmingham, and Ferdinand Morton, which was a Jell-O. Did he work with your show too?
Oh yeah.
Oh I didn't know that. He used to live with his grandmother in Bay St. Louis.
Oh really?
In Bay St. Louis, Mississippi. And the trumpets we had from time to time was Joe Oliver, Tom McCary, Ernest Punch Miller, Sidney Parris, Junior, he's called Gabriel, Louis Armstrong.
And Nelson. D.C. Nelson.
Now it was D.C.
Was that Oliver's nephew?
There was an Ornette, you know, son Nelson.
Well he passed as Joe Oliver's nephew. That's the same call then I'm thinking. Yeah, that little cornet player, little trumpet player, he was just learning then. I never knew him.
Well Lewis called him uncle too. Oh yes.
But Nelson was supposed to be his nephew.
Yes.
But he wasn't. Uh huh.
Well those were the uh...
And then the trombone players was Wilbur, D. Parris. Yes. D.Wilbur.
Yes. That's right. Was Oliver Everwith, Orr was with us one time. Eddie Orr, he was among the first.
Oh is that right? Yeah.
And then they had a man in New Orleans that was an all around man, played all instruments. He played trombone for us a while, Peter Bocard.
Oh yes, he's still active, he still plays trombone.
He's still there, yes.
He plays violins, still plays violins.
Yes, yes, yes. Play an instrument. Then Wilbur Parrish that she named.
Yes.
And what was the trombone player was at Peter Albert.
Dutre? Dutre?
Yeah.
You know Dutre? I never knew him, but I know of him.
Yes, Dutre?
Then the drummers that we had from time to time was Baby Dots and a boy named Happy. Yeah, I never did know any other names.
There were two Happys, one was called Red Happy and the other Black Happy. Yeah. Happy Bolton. Benny, Benny the drummer. Black Benny.
Black Benny, yes. Black Benny, that's the real deal.
The drummer Happy was at Happy Bolton, a very short fellow. I never knew him. Yeah. The other Happy is Happy Goldston. He still plays down there.
Oh, well this Happy must be dead.
Yes, that's Red Happy.
He was a kind of red, light-skinned fellow with freckles. Bolton, yeah.
He played with Joe Oliver and Ori.
That's right. He was considered one of the best drummers in town.
Yes, yes. In time.
Then there was a fellow called Two Bits.
Oh yeah, Bunk Johnson once mentioned him. I never...do you know his name?
Nothing but Two Bits.
Well, Two Bits. That's all Bunk called him, Two Bits. Two Bits, yeah.
Two Bits, yeah. That's our brother. Brought him up north, too. Yes, yes. He married in Lynchburg, Virginia. I guess he's still there.
Did you ever know Bunk Johnson? Oh yeah, surely.
Oh yeah.
Did you ever work with him, too?
Well, he worked with us only once. He was down in Houston, Texas, and he came over and played with us.
He went over to Texas around 1914, I think, and stayed over that way. Yeah.

We got some Texas musicians, too, from there, from Houston. L.C. Tolan, and Marquiva Spreex, and who else? I don't remember. Well, then there was a drummer we had called Tootinan, he was from Mobile. And another New Orleans boy was Ray Dugas. Yes, yes, yes.
Ray Dugas, yeah.
Heard the name, I never knew. He was a real light fellow. And Little Mac, we would call him. Yes. And Black Benny. Those were drums.
But did Black Benny travel with you? I didn't know he ever went anyplace except for him.
Yes, yes, we taken him. You are. Yes, he could. Mac would be the only one he'd go away with because he knew Mr. Mac would come back home.
I didn't think he ever went anyplace.
Yes, he did.
He was afraid he couldn't get back home. Most people tell that he just played bass drum, but he played the whole drum set. Oh, yes, yes, he was good.
I rented a set of drums to carry along with me so he'd have drums to play. He had a bass drum, but he didn't have the output, you know.

The funniest thing about it is when we came here with our band, we thought the band could set in the pit. We didn't know, you know, about the union. We had a union. And so they said, your band can't play. So Mac said, well, I'll put them on the stage. They're the best performers. They can play. Yes. And so that's what started. Then Bruce came in. You know Bruce? You heard of Bruce? I can't remember. He had his show too. Then he was the second with the orchestra on the stage.
Yeah, he fired up me out of New Orleans with him. Well, you see, I'll tell you what happened around 1914. I think the government called the red light district in New Orleans out of bounds for the
Army Navy. During the war.

Yeah, during the war. And all the night clubs couldn't do any business then. They closed up. So that's how we were able to get all these people to go out of town. They wouldn't have had anything else to do, would they?
No, because now we were at the Pete Lawless working there, Joe Oliver and Johnny Dodge and Mud Carey and oh, just the whole bunch. Yes. And they were going to take some of them to war too, wasn't it?
Well, they did it. They left town. It was made to leave for the afraid of that.
So many of them joined up with Mac, that's why they joined up.
Well, this place of Pete Lawless, was that the one at Marais and the Custom House? Yes, yes. I think Professor Minetta said he opened another place back on Villery someplace.
Villery, well that was a little theater.
He built for me. Oh, really? I didn't know about that. It was in a theater.
That was a little theater. Uh-huh. Really?
Yes. Where was that just about? On Claiborne, between the basin, the old basin up there, the new basin. That's the old basin.
Yeah. I can't think.
And Conti.
We're about in, I know about where it is.
Yeah. It's not there now, of course. There's a cemetery in there, of course. Oh, that was across the street.
Across the street from the theater. From the theater. Or rather, the theater was built across the street from the cemetery.

And Louis Armstrong, he was out to Miss Joseph's home. That was a home for bad boys. Yes, I remember. And then he would come to the cabaret at night and put on long pants and play with Joe in there, with sneaking plays. Uh-huh.

Well, at first, though, this man, Lou Rosen, we were talking about him, who was a, manager of the Dolphin Theater. He had a company there in Orleans called Lee's Creole Bells, run by Ed Lee. Well, Ed Lee had heard so much about us, he wanted to get us to work with him. So we did. And, uh, after he saw that I could produce shows, I was his producer. And I stayed with him. How long did we stay with Ed Lee up there for Lou Rose? Oh, years. Yes, three or four years. Every summer. You know, we just get tired of being black, like here's a monogram.

We just got tired. You know? They just keep you. Yeah. And the people would go to the show and say, is Mac and Mac here? No. Mac's Mary, no. Well, we're not coming. Then we have to come back. Just keep, just coming back, coming back, coming back. Yeah.
Yeah, we worked there at one lot, there at Louisiana Avenue and Howard, for 14 weeks. And then there was another man named Strohler. He was from Algiers, Mr. Strohler.
Yes.
And he built an air drone over on, on, Jackson.
Jackson and Robinson.
Jackson and Robinson. Yes, yes, uh-huh.
Did you have sort of a tent too, sometime that you traveled with?

Oh, this was a tent for Lou Rose. Yes, it was. Yes. And we worked around in this air drone for quite a while. And Louis then, and this little Mac, and little Georgia Gray, and, and Happy, they had a little quartet. Now, at this time, none of them were playing drums or horns.
That was the vocal part.

Yes. They'd come up there and sing, haven't you, night sound, why, you know, when I'd have them. And that's where I first met Louis. You went to work? Well, later on when he started playing the horn, then I used him too, you know. But he didn't take up this horn until after he went to this home. He did. And they'd give him these instruments, you know, in order to, you know.
And when we come to St. Louis here, here, I mean to St. Louis. I know, yes. Louis come up on a boat with the red, what's his name, red, that used to work on the boat? Oh yeah.
Oh yeah.
Oh, uh, uh, uh, fake marabout, maybe.
Yes, fake marabout. Yes, well we call him red marbles. Yes, fake marbles. Yes, fake marbles.

And when we come from the, was going to the theater, to rehearsal, there was Louis sitting on steps waiting. Oh right. We got off the boat sitting waiting for us and he played with us a while there and said, Louis. Yes. Uh huh, but he had to go back on the boat. Yes. But he waited there and waiting to see Mac and Mac. You know, there's so much to think about after you think back, but my goodness, there's things to be forgotten.

Well, we had no reason to mention them. Nobody talked to us about them. All those old times, they're all gone. So many of them. Yeah. And so, during this organizing, way back in, if we're talking too long, then let me know.
No, no, no. I don't want to take your whole afternoon, but if you have a few more minutes, I'd like to hear some more about the travels and all.

Sure. I used to, in organizing these shows, I'd always sit down and write my material. And so we had, everything we had was original. That's why we could come back and also stay so long whenever we'd play any game. But we always had something new to offer. And I was the originator, see, with her help. And she could always sing. I never was a singer.
I was wondering, because on the record, you all both sang some. If your act is mostly a comedy act or singing, or just what did you do?

I sang. And we sang together. Comedy songs, you know. But I could dance a little. But I was leading lady, you know. Well, you look pretty and dance a little and sing. But we did our act. We had an act. Not an act. Acts.
Oh, yes. The whole show.
Because when you go to New York, if you were doing vaudeville, when you go to New York...
Go ahead and answer that. I can turn this off for a minute. Unless you want to keep, one of you keep talking. It's all right.

When you go to New York, you know, you'd get a half of...the first half. Yes. Of the whole...the whole...the first half. And then somebody else had the second half. Well, then instead of us getting just the first half, we'd have the first half. And they'd say, can you change your act for the second half? Yes. Then can you change for next week? And would you see that in New York at the Lincoln Theater and Washington at the Howard Theater and all of those theaters. Well, instead of keeping us just the three days or four days, well, they'd keep us two and three weeks. Stay on. Uh-huh. And a southern act, too, you know.
That was Sister Foster.
What do you want? If you want to answer the phone, it's all right. I can turn this off for a while.
No, that's all right. It's gone now.
Oh. I was telling him about the vaudeville and String Beans.
Oh, yeah. Butler May. I read about him.
Yeah.
He was a great comic.

Yes. He said, Mac, come to New York. You come to New York. And that was 1914 when we went to New York. Yeah. And we were so scared, you know, that we were going to get fired, or canned, get the hook. You know, they had a hook that they would grab you. Oh, yeah, it is. Yeah. And the Whitman sisters, they were there with us. They were not there with us, but they were in New York.
Yes.

And they would come with the suitcases. So when they'd canned an act, all they had to do was come out the audience and come on, you see, ready. So we just thought that we were going to get, I did, not Mac. Mac was always, he said, just do the act like we've always did it. And I said, well, they don't have acts like that. He said, do the act like we've always done our act. And we did. And when the man come to the dressing room door and knocked, you know, I thought he was putting the pictures under the door. And he asked about the, for the next half.
Well, we had a repertoire of changes, you know.
Yes.

And we could always stay as long as we'd want. Usually we'd always get three or four weeks by being able to change our act. And those Northern acts, we called them Northern acts because they all turned their noses up at us at first, you know, when they saw it. But what a riot we were when we finished our act. Then they come in to try to be friends. And so they used to come around and pat you on the back there and tell you, I'll find you, oh, I really enjoyed your act. And once in 1911, that was right after the comet, Halley's Comet, we were in Atlanta.
Yes, yes, yes.
Yeah.
Mm-hmm.

And this is where we got the Mac and Mac from. We were at Bailey's and their builders is Mac Bride and Mac Bride, you know. But there was a man named George Freeman that was producing shows over on Peter Street in Atlanta. At a theater called the Paradise Theater. And when we went over there to work, he said, now, I'm going to have to change your billing. See, I tried to get that Mac Bride and Mac Bride, but that's too long. See, why not just call yourself Mac and Mac? Well, that's where it started. So George Freeman was the one that gave us that. Yeah. Good stuff.
Yes, yes.
I'm wondering back in those days, what kind of music or band did you carry, any band with you? Any of the New Orleans musicians that early, or when did they start going out with you?
Eddie Haywood used to play. Oh, Eddie Haywood. Eddie Haywood used to play for us in Atlanta, and Professor Lovey Austin's father was playing where? Chattanooga.
He was playing in Chattanooga.
Chattanooga, and Mandy that works on the television now. Mandy. Oh, yes. Who is she working with? Father Knows Best?
She worked with lots of different shows, Emerson, Andy, and different ones.
Well, Mandy, she was the mama. Well, now, she played piano in Annapolis. Oh, they had good piano players everywhere.
So, whoever in each city used their own musicians.
Yes, yes, yes. You didn't carry your own... No, not until we...
1918, about. Yes.
Well, 1914 was when we took out this... But now that it's time...
Oh, who went with you in 1914?
This is when we took Johnny Dodds and them around, but we didn't go directly to...
No, we didn't. We were taking Johnny Dodds and them in 1918.
Yes.
19... When the district closed in New Orleans for the Army, you know...
Yes.
They were going to take them to the Army. I do.
I don't know.
Do you remember? You know, Pete Lawless, they come around to the cabaret to get the... Mm-hmm. For them to sign up and all that. And so that's when they decided to go away. Yeah.
That was my... Well, what we wanted to say there in answer to Mr. Russell's question is that each theater had their own piano player and drummer. Yes. Some just a piano player.
Mm-hmm.

And we got to meet all these fellas. Oh, yeah. And after we started our own show, why a lot of times when we needed a piano player, they'd leave. They'd leave any one of them to leave any house to go traveling, you see. And so...
I just wondered if any of the men from New Orleans had gone with you as early as 1914, before Mudcary and Dodds?
Yes, the Bay St. Louis. Just over the Bay St. Louis.
Yes.
And up and down that coast from Mobile to New Orleans we played and up... coming up northward in Mississippi as far as Laurel, Mississippi. And then there. Yes.
Buddy Christian and Bud Scott. Yeah.
Well, did they tell you about the banjos we had from the time to... Oh, yes.
There's some banjos.

Yeah, we had a guitar and banjo and Buddy Christian. He could play the guitar too. And then there was John Lindsay and Bud Scott and James Arnold, who is here now. We call him banjo because he used to play the banjos. Oh, yeah. I don't remember that name. Bud Scott?
No, Bud Scott I remember. The other James... Arnold. Arnold.
John Lindsay.
I knew him.
He's dead now. And Bud Scott.
What was it? What did you used to call him? Tabitski?
Yeah. Yeah. Well, that was just a nickname they had. That was about the only banjos or guitars they had.
And then they called him Banjo. You might have heard him speak of banjo.
Well, one while they called this James Arnold, Kokomo. He played a lot of records. Yes. I knew a... Oh, sure.
Sure, you know Kokomo. I heard him with Johnny Doggs over at the 29... Yeah, sure. That's Kokomo, yeah. Sure. Uh-huh, yeah, that's him. He plays his own company, on guitar.
Where did he come from? Do you know where he came from? I never did know.
Not New Orleans, are we? No, no.
He was the original from New Orleans. Kokomo, yeah. He don't play anymore. No, he's got him a steel mill job. He's got him a steel mill job. He's got him a steel mill job.
He's got him a steel mill job. He's got him a steel mill job. He's a preacher now, I think.
Really? Yeah. There is another Kokomo, though.
Another fellow that called him. Yes, there's a later one. I wonder, did you notice much difference in the bands, the early bands, between the New
Orleans fellows and the other musicians up north or other places in the south? Was there a different beat? Oh, yes.
Oh, yes.

Well, you know, say the jazz originated, that kind of ragtime and all they called it then, started in New Orleans. I wondered if you found that same kind of music up north or other places too? No, no, no. No, no.

They didn't any take it up until those fellows from New Orleans began to spread out up this way. Chicago being the easiest way north, and most of them came here first. Yes. And then from here they branched out to Philadelphia, New York and places.
Mm-hmm.

And we found too that there are a lot of musicians that were already here that didn't know that, didn't have that beat, didn't understand what it was all about. A lot of them were puzzled. I wouldn't, some of them argued they wouldn't play. That's not a lot of junk, you know. But they all come to it. Yeah, Joe Oliver, he was the one that started it here almost. Him and Johnny Dodds and them.
Yes. That's why at the Lincoln Garden, I mean the Royal Garden, they would be so crowded, the musicians around looking and listening and learning.

Joe Oliver and them started it. Well, there was a couple of fellows around these other nightclubs too, like Jimmy Noon, Freddie, what was his name? Keppard maybe. Keppard. Freddie Keppard, yes. Did you ever work with him?
Yes. Oh, yes.
He traveled with us for a while. Oh, he did? Well, I didn't clap, Freddie Keppard, yes.
I never knew him, but I know his brother is still living there, a very nice guitar player. He plays guitar. Louis Keppard.
Because we were about the only ones that had a show down there, didn't we?
Yeah. Well, traveling shows would go anywhere out of the race of New Orleans and certainly.

And any time the musicians would, some of them would get hot-headed or something like that. We would, and we'd show, go back and show in New Orleans. Well, then we'd bring new ones out. Yes. Then eventually, when they come to the centers and they want to come back, we take them back. Always party friendly. Yeah.
Quite a few of them got their start with us. That is, the traveling start in a way. They were playing music.

I was wondering, some of the very first music you ever heard in New Orleans, Mrs. Mack, if you can remember the very first band or dance music or parade music, any kind of music, when you were a little girl. Oh my goodness, all my life.
All my life. I've been following during the funerals and go sad and come back just to skip anything. They still have those.
Oh, yes.
What's the name of some of those bands that played around them? Of course, we know about Joe Oliver and that bunch, but there was two or three fellas that had pretty good bands around them.
Buddy, Buddy, oh my goodness.
I used to hear you talk about this. I know all of them.
Peter Bocard, he was in the band too. He blew, for funerals he'd blow a horn.
Do you remember a band, a cornet player called Buddy Bolden? Oh, yes, sure, sure.
He died soon. Yes, he's been dead. He told me he was living with his sister now. He sent me there to the restaurant.

Yes, Punch is, right now he's actually living with his niece, his sister's daughter in New Orleans. His sister's out in the country. Uh-huh. But he looks quite well and he still plays. You've seen him? Yes. Oh, yes, I've seen him down to see me about two weeks ago.
Is that true?
Two weeks ago last Saturday, I guess.
Were you from New Orleans?
Oh, yes, I lived there now.
Well, you give our love to Punch and tell him we got this letter.
All right, maybe I'll be able to play this record for him too.
All right. He said, listen there, Miss Mary, Mr. Mike. That sure is Miss Mary.
Well, almost all those boys, those musicians who have, were calling that were really born out in Louisiana. And they'd come to New Orleans and build up into this, these names for themselves.
Yes, Punch was born, I think, in Raceland out there. Raceland. Raceland. And Marty Orr. And Marty Orr.
Was it?
Orr. Orr was born up in Laplace.
We passed through there, Max, and they looked like Jesus was coming through. A man who looked like Jesus.

That was Orr's brother. He heard the, you see, when we were going to some little town up in Louisiana to play the show, give a show and a dance. And we had Orr and Joe Oliver and Martin, Orr, pretty good sized band, about five, six, seven maybe. And when they got to this farm, this cane farm where Orr's brother lived, where they played some music, see. Oh yeah. And they'd come Orr's brother to run into the cane. That's what she's talking about. And he ran through the sugar cane, you know.
Parting the cane. Parting the cane coming through and had long beards. And somebody, I think it was Joe Oliver, said, well here comes Jesus. He looked just like Jesus.

I guess that's the brother that went to California. They had a chicken farm out there with Kidori until 1940 or so. And then his brother died that year, I think. Yeah. That's true. I was out there at that time. I think his sisters, all of his relatives mostly are dead now. Yeah. But he's still in San Francisco and still playing. I think he may go to Europe this summer. Well, anytime.
He's still active. I saw him in a movie here at the Indiana Theatre. It was a story of this Chicago clarinist. What is his name again?
Oh, oh, oh, oh, not you may know.
Oh, Benny Goodman. Benny Goodman.
Benny Goodman's story.
Yeah.
I never got to see that.
You didn't? No. Oh, he had a whole way in quite a few of those. What's this fellow's name in Philadelphia from the Orleans? George something. George Bishop, not Bishop.
George Bakay had been there, but he's dead now too. Oh, is that so?
They say he passed too.
Bishop Bishop, yes. And many of those old timers are gone now. Yes, yes, yes.

Yeah, we knew Sidney Bishop when he was a kid. Oh, yeah. But he was playing the clarinet then too. He had a whole piece of clarinet strung together with wire. He'd come down and beat a lot of them. They'd let him sit in there along with the police and run him out because he was a kid. He was a little kid, I guess, in short pants. Yeah, yeah, yeah.
Let's run him and Louis out there. Run him out.

We were talking about these towns going through like that. Now Punch, when he came into the Orleans, he played around with us. But they didn't recognize him so much because he hadn't been in the Orleans too long. And so he kind of palled around with us because we always accepted any performers, musicians, you know, and fix meals so they could have. And so he got to like us and when we had room for him, we took him on and carried him around with us for a while. He traveled with you then too?

Yes, he did. Because this record that you made, I think on the record label, it says recorded in New Orleans. So I thought maybe he didn't go out of the city with you. Oh, yes. He traveled with us. He went everywhere.
And then here he lived with us. Oh, here in Chicago. Yes. He lived right in the house with us.

But some of the records we made though were made in New York and Clarence Williams played for us. He happened to be there. Yes. He wasn't traveling with us at that time. But once we were here and needed a trumpet player and punch, we got left down south or something. Oh, he turned out to be a kind of boozer. That's what it was. And we had to let him go.
Mm-hmm.
Oh, I shouldn't say that. Well, we won't play that part for you. I'll just play the first part. But anyway, he...
I know I've heard that about him too, that part. But he doesn't drink now. He's three with that forever.

Well, that's what ruined his health anyway. We used to talk to him. Anyway, we left him. We were playing Texarkana, Texas. And he went to sleep in the pit. And that was too much. I was trying to play the show. He didn't. He'd bring his head. Sure didn't.
Tell him, all right, we're ready.

So when we got up here, we found he was in Houston, Texas. And we wired him. And he sent a wire back, said he'd like to come, but he didn't have a trumpet. So I told him, come on empty hands. We give him anyway. And we got here. I had a trumpet for him. I bought one hour, a pawn shop. And he stayed with us a long time after that. He's been right here in this house every time. He's a real meal with us. He'll be glad to hear from you.
Oh, yes.

And then we just got to, he writes to us all the time. Because he can always find us, but we can't find him. Yes, that's right. Because we have one address, you see. But he's a fine fellow, Punch. Oh, yes.

I've known him now just three years. I never could find him in the years I used to travel around. He was with a carnival. And I could never find him. He wasn't in Chicago when I'd come through here. Mm-hmm. But he came back to New Orleans about almost three years ago now.
Yes, I did.

And he's been working there sometimes as a musician. He had other jobs too. But now he'll be on the Social Security. He'll be able to get a pension from the Army too. He was in the Army, you know. Yes, yes.
He certainly was. He certainly was in the Army.

I was going to ask about when you would sing with the Oliver Band, can you remember some of the other songs? You mentioned the Royal Garden Blues. I know it's hard to remember all those titles, but what type of songs did you...
Oh, I just sing the blues, you know, plain blues, and Easy Rider, because, you see, I learned all those numbers at Hande's in the Memphis.
Oh, yes.
Mm-hmm.
You'd sing some songs that I wrote too, like the... Oh Me, Oh My blues now. Oh, yes. That's something I wrote about 50 years ago, which I probably said, oh, record it.
Oh, we had plenty of songs on the ground.
I've heard of that. Didn't somebody else record that? Somebody made a record. Henry Williams, he took lots of our... It must have been Henry Williams. Rubberlegs.
He took lots of our music, because he worked with our show, see. I've seen that title.
Uh-huh. Uh-huh. And there was My Heartbreaking Gal, a song of mine.
Oh, I wanted to ask you again to interrupt you. Oh, excuse me. The New Orleans, I mean the twist, Mary... 된 stuff with
twist. Twine. Was that a dance sort of? Yes, it was a dance. Everywhere they had a movement to it.
The chorus did that. It kind of descriptive thing. Yes. And the Devil Jazz, we had another number, the Devil Jazz. That was a number where the chorus, for every line that you do they
done the step for it. Yes. Of course. We didn't record that one though. I got done. I had every night, we didn't record.

So many good songs. Oh, I used to sing everything. Yes, I used to sing everything. With Joe's band, just anything they'd play, you know. Some of our music and... All the late popular songs, anything that they'd... Anything, yes. They'd play... And you'd sing a vocal chorus or two. Yes. Then you didn't sing just the vocal chorus, you sung the verse too. The verse too, yes. The verse and the chorus. You sing the verse and then you go on

with choruses, many choruses. Yes. At that time, such songs as A Good Man is Hard to Find, that was popular. Mm-hmm. And All Night Long, you know what I mean? Yes. Yes, I have the music. And it isn't what he's got that makes me love him,
it's the way he does. It isn't what he does that makes me love him, it's the way he does it. Yeah. And all those kind of numbers.
Jasper Taylor, whom I saw last night... Oh, yeah. ...said to ask you about the Robichaux's,
if you played there at the Lyric Theatre. Lyric Theatre, yeah. Robichaux? Show them Robichaux? Yeah.
Sure. Now, he had a whole band of New Orleans fellas there. Oh, yeah. So you didn't have your own band for that,

you would just go in and sing? Yes, we did. Now, when we... What did you do? When we go in, uh, uh, so the Lyric, or to any theatre that had a band, well then, their, their band would play their overture, and then our band would come. Oh, you still keep your own band? Oh, sure, yeah.

See, we'd be on stage. See, we'd be on stage. Yes. And that was a part of the show. Mm-hmm. And that was a big drawing. You always had your band then? Yes. Yes, don't care. But they had one. They were counted. We say we had 30 people, or 27 people, where the band was counted in as part of the show. Yes.

And Robichaux's music was kind of a classic kind, you know. Mm-hmm. He didn't, uh, like jazz. Yes, that's right. He didn't jazz much, you know. And any theatre that we went to that had an orchestra, when, uh, they played their overture. They threw in their wheelchairs. Mm-hmm. That's right. Uh-huh.
And Robichaux was crazy about our style, though, and our music. Yeah. He didn't sit back and pull it wrong. Yeah. That was a, you could see him shaking and laughing off. Oh, for sure.

I might ask you just a minute or two, Mr. Mack, about, uh, the music in Mobile. I've heard of the old Excelsior Brass Band, and, uh, we talked to Mr. Pope, not the, I can't think of his first name. Alexander Pope was the leader of the original band. Yeah. And I talked to his son, who's still living. He's about 80 years old now.

Ha, ha, ha. But, uh, do you remember that Excelsior Band? Yeah. Yeah. I remember them for the reason that, uh, uh, in Mobile, being born, they, you know, they, they lived, uh, uh, what they called the Creoles in Mobile. They were Creoles, you know. Yeah. Yeah. And, and... Yes, he's very light. Yeah, yeah. See, and they didn't really, uh, mix too much with the rest of the colored people. And so, that's why I remember them so well. But I think this fellow, one of the musicians, who was named Willie, Pope or something like that. I don't remember very well. And we had, uh, a fellow that later became one of, that was the leader of the Eureka Band, named Charlie Lipscomb. Oh, yes. I've heard of, uh, his name. Yeah. Well, he went, uh, on my first tour out of Mobile.

I believe he's dead. Somebody told me he was, uh, Cootie Williams' teacher, I believe, too. Yeah. Did you know Cootie Williams, who played with Ellington? Sure. I know him. There's another old man whom I didn't get to meet, who still is there. I'll meet him my next trip. They called him Chicken. Some people said they could only remember his name. No. It was Chicken. Do you remember that name?
No. Well, there was a fellow called Charlie Chicken Jones, but I think he's dead.
Oh, yeah. Chicken Jones. Chicken Jones. Chicken Jones. Uh-huh.

There was, uh, some old musicians there. Uh, well, my father used to run a barbershop on Davis Avenue right down. Oh, by the way, in Mobile, there's a man, uh, I don't know, he's probably gone too. His name was Charlie Schreiner, a John Furrier-German fellow. And he built the Pike Theater for me. I just went around the country and I was having people, but they liked me so well, they wanted me to stay around, you see. And so, he said, when you come back here, I'm going to have a theater. I'm building it just because of you. And he used to loan me money too, whenever I was organizing, needed costumes and things. And I could go to Charlie Schreiner, you're in a town, a town saloon. And, uh, on account of me being always able to make enough money to pay him back, he got the idea, well, if you make money like that, I don't feel like that. Yeah. And so, all these musicians, Mobile musicians, they, they, uh, got their idea of jazz from Buddy Christian. He came over there over there. From Buddy Christian? From Buddy Christian. He'd come to Mobile and talk to the Mobile musicians how to play that style. And, of course, Johnny King, he went to New Orleans, lived a while, and he was a Mobile boy.

How did those bands compare with the New Orleans bands when you heard them later? That is, the brass band, did they swing a good deal, you know? I mean, on the street, like the funerals, you talk about coming back, you know, where they'd really swing now. Yeah, yeah. Did the Mobile bands play that same style?

They picked that up and got that out, yeah, after, like I say, the King and Christian, they kind of give them a few lessons in it, what it was all about. I was trying while talking to think of a fellow named, uh, Ed Jones, I think. He used to lead his band. He was the original, the leader of the original Eureka band, Ed Jones. In Mobile? In Mobile. And he...
Was that Eureka or Excelsior, do you remember?
No, Excelsior was this, uh... That was the Pope's band. Pope's band.
And they had a Eureka band, too. Yes. I didn't know it.
And Ed Jones used to lead the band with a baritone horn. One of them upright things, you know. Yes. And I was just over there. He did the flake jazz.
Mm-hm.

You could hear him for miles and miles. When they were coming back from the funeral. Mm-hm. And they'd step it up. About stuff like stuff stuff like stuff stuff like stuff like stuff stuff like stuff had a band. One time he had the Eureka band. But there always was in Mobile the same thing. Whatever happened in New Orleans, it would later get to Mobile. Like the Mardi Gras and everything.

Same type of music and dance bands too. Dance bands and everything. I was going to ask Mrs. McBride a little bit more about the early bands when you were even a little girl, the first dances you'd go to or when you'd hear if you can remember Buddy Bolden's band at all.
I do remember, yes. That was the band then. Because the trombone... I can't think of the name.
Do you remember there were a couple of trombonists that worked with Buddy Bolden, they tell me I didn't know them. Frankie Doosan. From Frankie Doosan, yes.
Oh, I see why.
My dear, I was trying to think. He looked like a Mexican. Frankie Doosan.
I've seen his picture, yes.

Yes, yes. He was of a dark complex with straight hair. Frankie Doosan. He came from Algiers too, Professor. Why, I know the whole family. I'm trying to think of all of them. But I just can't think it's been so long in no years. Frankie Doosan.

A banjo player, but I don't think he was from Algiers, the Brock Mumford. Who? Mumford, Brock. Brock? And then there was the Lorenzo Stahl. Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah. But they were from over on the other side, uptown on the other side of the river.

Yeah, well I knew Lorenzo Stahl for a pretty period too there, but he played with us once too. I think he went up on this trip when you said about, oh, his brother coming through the cane. Uh-huh. I think Lorenzo Stahl was with him. He was with Oliver. Oh, he was?
Yes, sure. Lorenzo, yeah.
Are you bringing up names? Of course, you were still down there, living there.
He's not living, but people tell me about him.

Oh, they're down there, but my goodness. We'd have to go way back. Now, as much as I followed the band, why, if somebody died, we'd wait for the funeral, for the band to be played behind them. And I'd know everybody that played in the band, but I can't think of them now.
Well, do you remember the Johnson brothers over in Algiers, Yank and Buddy Johnson, the trombone?
That's who I was trying to say, who played trombone? Buddy Johnson, Little Shortfella. Do you remember them, Matt? Yeah, I remember Buddy Johnson.
Yank? Yeah, I know all those fellas, knew them then.
Yank was a drummer. Yeah. Yank played drums.
I thought he played trombone too later, I think. Yes, yes.
But I think they both... Yank was the long-haired one. Mm-hmm.
I never knew them myself. Well, we knew them. I remember them now.

I know Buddy, I know Buddy Johnson, Little Shortfella, he was. Then Yank, his brother was bad. Yank was the bad boy. When we went to school together, he had long heads. Mm-hmm. Yeah. Yeah. And he was the kind of thing. Well, I reclaimed.
Well, we've had no reason or occasion to bring up all those names, and so you do forget. Yeah, certainly. But when we hear him again, remember, well, I used to know him. Sure, sure.
And the Lindsays, Johnny Lindsays.
Yes. And, Burbeth. Their father. Burbeth. Yeah. They lived right around the corner. Mm-hmm. Mamie, the sister, she went away with us. Yeah.
Mamie, the children did. Went to, in Memphis. She stopped in Memphis, didn't you? Was it Memphis? It was.
It wasn't, but she'd come back there. She stopped there.
Yeah.

Can you tell me, um, if, uh, Johnny Lindsay, I know his dad died 1951, I believe, up here, when I was here, I knew him, but his brother, somebody told me he had a brother still living here. Do you know?
He has a brother.
Is that Herbert? Herbert, Herbert.
Is he still here? He's here somewhere. He was on South Parkway the last time I heard from him. I saw him. Buzzy saw him, my brother. Yeah. You see, my brother, he knows, see everybody from home.
I wish I could find him sometime and interview him. I won't be able to do this trip, I suppose, but next trip, maybe.
You see, there were so many, uh, that has passed. Now, we have a theatrical chair club here.
Yes.

Uh, I know who? We met at, uh, what's his name's house the other night? Uh, Jasper Taylor tells me about, tells me about that. We met, we met at his house, and Jack L. Cooper, well, he's our business manager, you know? Yes. And, uh, there's so many old performers there, but there's none as old as, hardly as us, you know, as together. But Butterbeams and Susie, and they are out of town, you see.
Oh, are they still, uh, around Chicago sometimes, or no? Yes. They live here. They live on.
Uh-huh. 3322 Calumet Avenue.
I've seen them several times on the stage. Yeah. See Apollo Theater in New York, and once in Pittsburgh, too.
I think they're in Pittsburgh now, or something, they went to Pittsburgh.
Now the Whitman sisters, they're, they're about the oldest, and like us, you know. Uh-huh.
What was this, uh, fellow named, I think he was a trombonist, too. What was their name, Dutray? Dutray, yeah.
He bought a black villain?
Dutray. Yeah.
You know Dutray?
I mean, he bought.

He played over at, uh, uh, Lincoln Garden with us. Yeah, yeah. Yeah, he bought that 49th in, uh, in Michigan. That big, black villain. Well, Margaret, Margaret. That big corner. But he lost it. He passed, you know. Yes, he's dead.
And his brother, Sam, is dead now, too. He played clarinet. Yeah. Uh-huh.
Yeah. Jimmy Newman, is he, where, he's here.
He died in California, 1944. Oh.
Yeah. He used to play with us at the Cabaret, too. At the Dreamland, yeah.
Uh-huh.
And then up on, uh, 55th Street.

And there was a bunch over to the Deluxe that worked over there. That's where Freddie, uh, Keppert? Keppert. Keppert was. He was, uh, it was an upstairs nightclub, remember? Uh-huh. Up over to States Theater? Yes.

Oh, can you tell me a little bit more about Jolly Roll Martin before we quit? I don't want to take your whole afternoon, but if you can, uh, when he comes to the New Orleans, uh, when he traveled with you, you say he came from, uh, around Bay St. Louis. Yeah.
Well, he didn't come up here with us, but he'd go into New Orleans, and up and down the coast, Scranton, and, well, obviously. And then he lived with us, you know.
We had always kept house, you see, and then, for fun, we just lived there, you know.
And his grandmother, we always lived with her when we'd go to Bay St. Louis, the room, you know, she'd do this room. And we got to, uh, that's how we got to know Jolly Roll.
Yes.

And, uh, he went around in Mississippi and, and, you know, Spartan, Louisiana with us from time to time. And he was a fine kid, and he always did the things that he recorded later when he got to be a young man. He played all that stuff when he was a kid. stuff like stuff like
the pearls and the jelly roll blues and the whining boy.
Yeah, the jelly roll blues. King Porter, did he know?
He hesitated, must have hesitated. And I used to use that in the show, you remember?
Yes, all those numbers.

About what year was that? Can you remember when? 9 and 10, 99, 1910. When he was along the Gulf Coast with you? Yes, yes. One other man I was going to ask about, Tony Jackson, if you ever worked with him or remember?
Yes, it was a pint, a half pint?
Tony Jackson, not, not, uh... Not Frank Jack... Oh, yeah, half pint. Tony Jackson was a piano player.
Uh-huh, I was thinking about this little Jackson.
Oh, yeah, half pint Jackson, yes.
Tony Jackson, yeah.
He was from New Orleans. Yeah. And he was, uh, he used to play at the Deluxe, too. He used to sing, he used to sing a song called, uh...
He wrote Pretty Baby was one of his numbers. Do you remember that?

Yeah, well this thing, I don't know whether he wrote it or not, uh, and I can't even think of it now, but I have a... After a while or all the while or something about it with the word while in it. Mm-hmm. And the cold winter it blow, snow and blow, you know, I remember some of the rhymes. Yeah, snow and ice, maybe.
Yeah, and the ice and the snow.
Remember the stuff?
Yeah, it was published. I have the music for it. Yeah, yeah. But there was another name they used for it, too, and I forget that name, too.
Well, Tony Jackson, the first time I heard it, that's what he was singing. He sang that here at the Deluxe.
You know it's good for people to think of those things when you can't think now. Who would ever think of Tony Jackson, all of them?
I would, I would.
Maybe just as it would run across your mind, you know?
Yes, yes.
And all of them.
Well, how did I think of all these names? Now, yes, there's about 20 names down here that I'd never think of otherwise.

You have a good memory to remember those fellas because they were just sort of, you know, worked along with you, the show, you know, like hired help, you might say, and they weren't a real part of the show always. I mean, they weren't as important as the singers and dancers, and I'm surprised you remembered all those musicians. It's really wonderful. Well, I don't want to bother you more. We're just about out of this tape here, so if you don't mind, I'd like to snap a picture. You don't have to worry about being dressed up or anything. Oh! Just have a picture here at home. They can tell us at home.
Oh, what? Don't take no picture here. Well, all right.
I'll take it. Take Matthew. I'll take you by and then do you, Mr. Matt.
Well, I mean, you don't look bad at all. You're not looking bad at all. No, you don't look bad. I mean, if it's a bus picture, you don't have to show it.
We can have the background, you know, so they can see it's in your home. They'll know it's no studio. Take it in the kitchen, even. Well, take it in the usual place.
Yeah, any place.
Well, I want to have my dressing in. Tip stuff
